title: Brass nerve vs. shrinking back
core: All of these place someone on one axis: how far you push yourself forward in a room, and whether the room licenses it. At one end the person takes more than their standing allows; at the other they take less than their standing permits; in the middle sits the one behavior everyone approves of. The trap is that most of these words aren't descriptions of the act at all — they're the observer's verdict on it, so the same nerve gets called courage, audacity, or temerity depending on who's narrating.

words.nuance: The only one on the nerve side that can be a compliment — it withholds the verdict and lets the sentence supply it. Applause or gasp, both are available; every other bold word here has already decided.

The offence is specifically the *visibility*: done in the open, with no cover story and no flinch. It implies contempt for the onlooker — hiding would have conceded the rule mattered. Also the only one that verbs (**brazen it out**).
A noun, and the charge is shamelessness — the barefaced calm where a blush belonged. Lives inside "had the effrontery to —," and whatever follows is something the speaker finds indefensible.

The neighbouring noun, but the charge is *presumption*, not shamelessness: you addressed someone you should have deferred to. The private questioning the general has **temerity**; the general charging the hill has courage. Standing, not nerve, decides which.

The mildest offence here and the only one about *manner*: lippy, cheeky, grinning at a superior as though rank didn't exist. Spoken downwards — by teachers, magistrates, outraged fathers — and it slightly dates the speaker.

The hinge: full force, nothing overstepped. Nobody's rank is violated and nobody is owed a blush, which is why it's the one word here HR will print. Passive says nothing, **assertive** says it plainly, aggressive says it at your expense.
The shrinking is caused by self-doubt, not fear — you suspect your claim isn't good enough to press. Cooler than *insecure*, and the speaker usually thinks you're wrong about yourself.

Here fear is the engine: shrinking, hedging, trembling before a decision that needs making. Bookish and faintly withering, which is why it fits a committee that won't commit better than a nervous child.

No fear and no self-doubt — simply a settled preference for staying out of the light. The gentlest word in the group and mildly approving: the **retiring** colleague does the work and lets someone else present it.
The shrinking is staged. Reticence chosen and displayed so you'll notice the withholding and press harder — a CEO **coy about the numbers** isn't bashful, she's managing you.

exam_note: Watch the noun slot: "had the ___ to" takes both effrontery and temerity, and the sentence must tell you whether the sin was shamelessness or overstepped rank — and remember audacious and coy carry no fixed verdict, so the surrounding clause, not the word, sets the sign.
